newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Gazprom may see challenges in capital search.
newsitem.headline: Gazprom may see challenges in capital search.

text.p: Russian gas monopoly Gazprom, which intends to tap capital markets for up to $3 billion, offers investors strong credibility based on its size and power but has blots on its record, economists said on Monday.
Foreign investors have a strong appetite for Russia and RAO Gazprom should benefit from its high profile, said Renaissance Capital gas analyst Yuri Butayev.
"Gazprom has shown it can get as much as it needs."

He said investors would snap up both a $1 billion or more Eurobond and $500-$1 billion in convertible bonds to be offered in the next six months, despite some problems with foreign-traded shares and huge tax debts.

"The Eurobond yield will probably be the same or a little higher than the Russian sovereign," he said, referring to the Russian Federation's five-year $1 billion bond launched last November at 345 basis points over U.S. 5-year Treasuries.

Dutch bank ABN-Amro and U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs have been mandated to arrange a $2-3 billion financing programme, including $500-$1 billion in short-term bridge financing, ABN-Amro's country manager for Russia said on Monday.
Gazprom's financial adviser in Russia confirmed that such plans existed.
Butayev pointed to Gazprom successes this year in raising credits from commercial banks.
Dresdner bank in February led a consortium offering a $2.5 billion credit with eight year maturity at an interest rate of two percent over London Interbank Offered Rates (LIBOR).

A Deutsche Bank syndicate lent a further 1.5 billion marks and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development $300 million, for pipeline maintenance and helping to build the $40 billion Yamal pipeline to Europe, a multi-decade project.

But Gazprom is one of Russia's top tax debtors, with government debts of about $2.5 billion and a top target of reformer First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov who has often personally intervened in Gazprom, 40 percent owned by the state.
Foreign investors may force Gazprom to pay a premium on its Eurobond because of its delays paying its taxes, said Creditanstalt research director Tom Balestrery.
"It has yet to prove its ability to service its own existing debt," he said.

ABN-Amro officials declined to give details of the convertible bond, but share analysts said it would almost certainly convert into an American Depositary Share (ADS), the only equity instrument Gazprom allows foreigners to trade.

The ADS trades at almost three times the price of the underlying shares it covers, and Balestrery said investors might require a premium from Gazprom for buying bonds convertible into premium-priced shares.
"The true key to success is at what price it will convert -- the current ADS price or closer to the local price?"

The ADS was launched last October at $15.75 and covers 10 underlying shares. The ADS, which did not trade on Monday, a British bank holiday, closed at $17.50 on Friday. Underlying shares on the Russian Trading System closed on Monday at $0.668.

Gazprom has made new efforts recently to approach foreign shareholders and is trying to increase transparency in terms of publishing financial results, soon to be audited to Western standards, and company plans.

But it is still far behind other major Russian companies, such as oil company LUKoil, which has a larger market capitalisation than Gazprom, partly attributable to a stock price boosted by substantial foreign investment.
LUKoil last week announed a convertible bond on five percent of its shares that Balestrery predicted would be priced to yield less than Gazprom's. LUKoil also has floated a convertible bond before.
"Gazprom officials are seeing the market makes the decisions," Balestrery said.
--Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520
